title: How do supermarkets make money, and what matters in a retail case?
description: Grocery retail economics for case interviews: thin margins, basket size, footfall, sales per square foot, private label and online delivery costs.
hook: Supermarkets make money by selling huge volumes at a thin gross margin and keeping store, staff and supply chain costs tightly controlled, so that a few cents of profit on each dollar of sales adds up. Because operating margins are only a few percent, small shifts in price, product mix, waste or labour can halve or double profit, and that sensitivity is what most retail cases test.
body:
The basic equation

Revenue = shopping trips × average basket. Trips come from footfall (how many people visit) and frequency; the basket comes from items per trip × average price per item. Profit is then gross margin (sales minus what the grocer paid suppliers) minus the costs of running stores, distribution, online fulfilment and head office.

Margins really are thin. Tesco, the UK's largest grocer, reported an adjusted operating margin of 4.3% for its 2025/26 financial year (Tesco preliminary results). The market is also concentrated: Kantar's December 2025 figures put Tesco at 28.7% of the British grocery market and the four largest grocers together at about two-thirds (Kantar). Large chains use that scale to negotiate with suppliers, which is why the push and pull with brands shows up in consumer goods cases too.

The levers

  • Footfall and basket size: how often people come and how much they buy each time.
  • Mix: fresh food, ready meals and own-label usually earn more per dollar than branded staples, and promotions earn less.
  • Private label: the retailer's own brand often earns a higher margin per item than the big brands, and gives it leverage in supplier negotiations.
  • Shrinkage and waste: theft, damage and food thrown away. These cut profit without ever showing up in sales.
  • Labour and space: labour hours per $1,000 of sales and sales per square foot show which stores and aisles work hardest.

A worked example: one basket, then one price cut

Take an illustrative store with an average basket of $50. The grocer pays suppliers $37 for those products, so gross profit is $13, a 26% gross margin. Store staff, rent, energy, distribution, shrinkage and central overhead come to $11.50 per basket, leaving $1.50 of operating profit, a 3% margin.

A competitor cuts prices and the client considers a 2% cut. That is $1 off every basket, so operating profit per basket falls from $1.50 to $0.50, a two-thirds drop if nothing else changes. That is the headline risk. But how many extra baskets would restore profit? It depends on which costs are fixed.

Say $2.50 of the $11.50 rises with each basket (card fees, bags, some labour, waste) and $9.00 is fixed at current volume. The store serves 15,000 baskets a week ($39M a year).

  • Contribution per basket before the cut: $50 − $37 − $2.50 = $10.50. After: $49 − $37 − $2.50 = $9.50.
  • Fixed costs: 15,000 × $9.00 = $135,000 a week. Weekly profit today: 15,000 × $1.50 = $22,500.
  • Baskets needed after the cut: ($22,500 + $135,000) ÷ $9.50 = about 16,580, so 10.5% more baskets.

That is the real question for the client: will a 2% price cut bring 10.5% more shopping trips, or will the competitor simply match it? Often it will not, especially if the competitor matches, which is one reason grocers tend to concentrate price cuts on the items shoppers notice most rather than across the whole store.

Online delivery

Online orders add a separate set of costs: picking, packing and the van. If the average online order is $80 at a 25% gross margin, gross profit is $20. If picking and delivery cost $15 per order, only $5 is left before any store or head-office costs. That is why grocers charge delivery fees, set minimum baskets and push customers towards cheaper delivery slots.

Typical retail case questions

  • Why has our margin fallen while sales grew? (mix, promotions, waste, labour)
  • How should we respond to a discounter entering our market? (see competitive response cases)
  • Should we launch a premium own-label range?
  • Should we open dark stores for fast delivery?

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "Sales are up, so we should look at costs. Maybe rent has gone up."
Strong: "Sales grew 3% but profit halved, so with margins this thin I'd first check gross margin. A shift towards promotions or a rise in waste could explain it without any change in store costs."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming more sales means more profit. Promotion-led growth can add revenue and destroy margin.
  • Ignoring shrinkage. Theft and waste are invisible in the sales line. Always ask.
  • Treating every cost as variable. Rent and most store staffing do not fall when a store is quiet, so volume changes hit profit harder than you expect (see operating leverage).
  • Mixing margin and markup. A product bought for $37 and sold for $50 has a 26% margin but a 35% markup. Be clear which one you mean (margin versus markup).

Practise

1. A store's sales are flat but operating profit has halved. What do you ask for before suggesting a marketing campaign?

Show the answer

Gross margin percentage over time (and whether mix has shifted to promotions or low-margin lines), waste and shrinkage, labour hours per $1,000 of sales, and energy, rent and distribution costs per store. Marketing does nothing if the problem is margin or cost.

2. A branded cereal sells for $3.00 and the grocer pays $2.40 for it. A new own-label version sells for $2.50 and costs $1.50. If 30 of every 100 brand buyers switch to own label, what happens to profit on those 100 shoppers?

Show the answer

Brand profit per unit: $0.60. Own-label: $1.00. Before: 100 × $0.60 = $60. After: 70 × $0.60 + 30 × $1.00 = $42 + $30 = $72. Profit rises 20% even though revenue falls (30 × $0.50 = $15 less). Watch the supplier's reaction, though.

3. Store A has 40,000 square feet and $30M of sales. Store B has 25,000 square feet and $21M. Which works its space harder?

Show the answer

A: $30M ÷ 40,000 = $750 per square foot. B: $21M ÷ 25,000 = $840. B works harder, but check gross margin and rent per square foot before concluding it is more profitable.

Where to practise next

Work through the Meadowlane Grocers case, where sales rose but profit halved, and the FreshMart case on a hard discounter entering the market. The profitability case guide gives you the full method.
